models.family: engineered leaf descriptors plus unsupervised clustering
models.purpose: Describe leaf shape with four numerical features and partition 32 leaves without prespecifying botanical classes.
models.summary: Leaf index, approximate area, a centroid-distance serration ratio, and leaf extended angle form a four-feature vector that is clustered in R into four groups.

variables.definition: Ratio of leaf length to leaf width.
Product of measured leaf length and width.
Ratio of mean centroid-to-concave distance to mean centroid-to-convex distance.
Angle formed by extending the lower leaf margins.
Distance between two points on the leaf image.
Centroid of the segmented leaf.
The i-th concave point on the leaf margin.
The j-th convex point on the leaf margin.
Number of concave margin points.
Number of convex margin points.
One of four clusters produced from the feature vectors.

governing_equations.label: eq1
governing_equations.purpose: Quantify margin serration relative to the leaf centroid.

equation_status.reason: The NR equation is printed on page 5; clustering is described algorithmically rather than by an objective or distance equation.

objectives: Produce a compact numerical leaf-shape representation.
Discover leaf groups without a prespecified class count.
constraints: Only 32 of 55 literature images are clustered.
Leaf area is approximated by length times width.
The cluster count is interpreted visually after fitting.

details: Four features are measured for each of 32 leaves.
Image scale, segmentation, distance metric, linkage, and cut criterion are not reported in the body.
This is a static clustering task.

parameter_estimation.method: Feature values are calculated from literature images; clustering settings are delegated to unreported R code in the appendix.

steps: Measure LI, approximate area, NR, and LEA.
Assemble four-feature vectors for 32 leaves.
Run cluster analysis in R 2.13.1.
Cut and display the result as four groups.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: No clustering objective, stopping criterion, stability analysis, or random seed is reported.

assumptions: The four descriptors retain the shape distinctions relevant to classification.
Literature images are comparable despite unreported scale and segmentation.
Visual similarity within the four clusters represents a meaningful class structure.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The clustering cannot be reproduced uniquely without preprocessing, feature scaling, algorithm, distance, linkage, and cut settings.

models.computational_cost: Unreported; standard hierarchical clustering would require at least pairwise comparisons over the sample set.
strengths: Avoids imposing labels before exploratory grouping.
limitations: Cluster validity is judged visually.
The method and preprocessing are underspecified.
No botanical reference labels or stability metrics are used.

models.purpose: Assign eight additional leaves to the four cluster-derived classes and use the assignments as a model check.
models.summary: Four engineered descriptors are min-max normalized, used to train a four-layer BPNN on 32 cluster-labeled samples, and applied to eight selected test leaves.

variables.definition: Unscaled LI, area, NR, or LEA value.
Minimum value of a feature in the sample.
Maximum value of a feature in the sample.
Feature scaled to the interval from zero to one.
Normalized LI, area, NR, and LEA for one leaf.
Cluster-derived training label.
BPNN class prediction for a new leaf.

governing_equations.purpose: Scale every predictor to zero through one before training.

equation_status.reason: The normalization equation is printed; network activations, loss, update equations, and decision rule are omitted.

objectives: Classify new leaves into the four discovered groups.
Check whether the cluster labels can be reproduced from the four descriptors.
constraints: The training labels are outputs of the preceding clustering rather than independent botanical truth.
The test set contains eight selected images.
Training uses 1000 epochs, learning rate 0.06, goal 0.01, and minimum gradient 1e-20.

details: Thirty-two cluster-labeled samples initialize training and eight samples are reserved for testing.
The paper does not define the selection seed, network weights, activation functions, class encoding, or stopping outcome.
Training terminates by software criteria rather than a physical equilibrium.

parameter_estimation.method: MATLAB BPNN training with stated epoch, display, learning-rate, goal, and minimum-gradient settings; architecture details conflict with the claimed BPNN terminology.

steps: Normalize each descriptor.
Use 32 cluster-labeled samples for training.
Train the network with the stated MATLAB parameters.
Predict four-class labels for eight held-out leaves.
Compare predictions visually with analogous cluster images.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Training stops at 1000 epochs, goal 0.01, or minimum gradient 1e-20; the realized stopping condition is not reported.

assumptions: Cluster labels are valid supervised targets.
The eight test leaves are independent and randomly selected.
Min-max ranges estimated from the sample apply to future leaves.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: Hyperparameters are partly stated, but absent weights, seed, activation functions, label encoding, and an independent ground truth prevent reproduction and valid accuracy estimation.

models.computational_cost: Unreported; the paper notes excessive runtime for large leaf collections but gives no complexity, hardware, or timing.
strengths: States several training hyperparameters and a normalization formula.
limitations: Seven-of-eight visual agreement is not a valid independent test of cluster labels.
Test selection and ground truth are undocumented.
The described hidden layer and decision layer do not clearly match a conventional BPNN.

models.family: three-dimensional geometric projection and polygon overlap
models.purpose: Quantify how leaf narrowness, phyllotaxis geometry, light direction, petiole length, inclination, and internode spacing affect unshaded leaf area.
models.summary: Four identical rhombic blades on two distichous layers are projected along parallel rays; translated polygons yield overlap area and the effective area ratio.

Total blade area not shaded by the upper layer.

Projected y coordinate on the horizontal plane.
Zero coordinate on the projection plane.
Altitude angle of sunlight.
Horizontal direction angle of sunlight.
Vertical separation between neighboring leaf layers scaled by leaf area.
Horizontal shadow displacement in x for the 45-degree example.
Horizontal shadow displacement in y for the 45-degree example.

governing_equations.purpose: Define the fraction of total blade area that remains unshaded.

equation_status.reason: EAR and the projection/displacement equations were visually checked; the long piecewise overlap expressions are poorly typeset and are not normalized here.

objectives: Calculate overlap and effective area for horizontal and inclined blades.
Compare overlap sensitivity across leaf geometry and light direction.
constraints: Only four identical unit-area rhombic blades on one vertical distichous shoot are modeled.
Rays are parallel and blades are flat and infinitesimally thin.
Neighboring branches and nonparallel light are excluded.

details: Two upper and two lower leaves form the base geometry.
Angles and scaled lengths are restricted to the ranges listed in Table 1.
The model computes static projected overlap.

parameter_estimation.method: The analysis sweeps geometric inputs rather than estimating parameters from observations.

steps: Construct rhombic blade coordinates.
Project upper blade vertices along the solar direction.
Compute translated polygon intersections with lower blades.
Subtract overlap from total area.
Sweep angles and scaled lengths in MATLAB.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Direct geometric calculation; no iterative convergence criterion applies.

assumptions: Blades are identical unit-area rhombi.
The shoot is vertical and has negligible radius.
Petiole and shoot shading, curl, thickness, and neighboring branches are negligible.
Sunlight is parallel.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The projection is reproducible, but the printed piecewise overlap formula, polygon cases, and inclined-blade implementation are not fully specified or tested against measured shadows.

models.computational_cost: Unreported; direct polygon intersection is small for four blades, while parameter sweeps scale with the product of sampled input grids.
strengths: Defines a decision metric before deriving geometry.
Makes light direction and three-dimensional projection explicit.
Includes parameter sweeps and a sensitivity table.
limitations: The biological system is reduced to one branch and four idealized blades.
No measured overlap or irradiance validates EAR.
The piecewise overlap derivation omits intermediate geometry and code traceability.
missing_details: Resolution of the printed piecewise formula

models.purpose: Estimate illumination as a function of vertical depth and horizontal distance from the trunk.
models.summary: Jackson's exponential vertical attenuation is multiplied by a linear radial term to form a two-dimensional canopy-light surface.

variables.definition: Illumination at a canopy location.
Light intensity above the canopy.
Tree-dependent attenuation coefficient.
Depth below the canopy top.
Tree-dependent coefficient for radial light variation.
Distance from the trunk within the crown.

governing_equations.source_expression: I = I0 (1 + alpha D) exp(-k l)
governing_equations.purpose: Add a linear radial variation to vertical attenuation.

equation_status.reason: Both the Jackson baseline and modified two-dimensional equation were visually checked on pages 24-25.

objectives: Represent vertical and horizontal light variation in a crown.
Supply local illumination to the leaf-size model.
constraints: Illumination depends only on height and trunk distance.
The radial correction is linear.
Other environmental resources are assumed abundant.

details: I_0 is specified at the canopy surface.
The radial domain needed to keep 1+alpha D physical is not stated.
The model is a static spatial field.

parameter_estimation.method: The paper says alpha and k can be estimated from illumination at selected canopy locations but gives neither observations nor fitted values.

steps: Specify I_0, alpha, and k.
Evaluate the equation over a grid of l and D.
Plot the MATLAB surface.
Compare its tendency qualitatively with an apple-tree curve from prior work.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Closed-form grid evaluation; no iterative convergence criterion applies.

assumptions: Light at a location is determined only by canopy depth and radial distance.
Jackson vertical attenuation transfers to this tree.
Horizontal variation is adequately linear.
Water, carbon dioxide, and nutrients are nonlimiting.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: No calibration observations, objective, fitted coefficients, uncertainty, or quantitative validation metric are supplied.

models.computational_cost: Linear in the number of spatial grid points; grid resolution and runtime are not reported.
strengths: Extends a cited vertical model with an explicit radial term.
Produces a simple handoff variable for leaf growth.
limitations: The sign and physical range of alpha are not constrained.
Validation is a qualitative curve-tendency comparison.
No canopy geometry or local leaf density enters the field.

models.purpose: Map local illumination to a bounded mature leaf blade area with a minimum survival-light threshold.
models.summary: A logistic-like differential equation replaces time and the usual size-proportional growth term with illumination, then imposes zero leaf area below a critical intensity.

variables.definition: Blade area at illumination I.

equation_status.reason: The differential equation and piecewise solution were visually checked on pages 26-27.

objectives: Bound leaf area by a species maximum.
Represent the failure of leaves to survive below critical illumination.
Convert the light field into a spatial leaf-size surface.
constraints: S is zero below I_0 and approaches K as illumination increases.
Only illumination varies; other growth constraints are held adequate.
K is constant for a species.

details: S(I_0)=S_0 at the critical viable illumination.
S=0 below I_0 and S is bounded above by K.
The response saturates toward K at high illumination.

parameter_estimation.method: No values or estimation data are reported for K, r_0, I_0, or S_0.

steps: Evaluate local I from the light-distribution model.
Return zero if I is below I_0.
Otherwise evaluate the closed-form saturation response.
Plot S over canopy depth and radius.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Closed-form evaluation; saturation toward K is analytic rather than iterative.

assumptions: Illumination is the limiting driver of within-tree leaf-size variation.
A modified logistic form remains valid when time is replaced by illumination.
A hard survival threshold adequately represents weak-light mortality.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: Four free parameters and the upstream alpha and k are not estimated; no leaf-area-by-light observations test the functional form.

models.computational_cost: Constant per canopy location after illumination is known; grid size and runtime are unreported.
strengths: States a bounded response and limiting cases.
limitations: Replacing time and size-proportional growth with illumination lacks a derivation.
The discontinuity at I_0 is not reconciled unless S_0 is zero.
No coefficients or actual leaf-area validation are provided.

models.family: crown-solid volume times attenuated mass density
models.purpose: Estimate total leaf mass from crown height and mean crown radius using candidate geometric solids.
models.summary: Six solid approximations convert crown dimensions to volume; volume is multiplied by a literature leaf-mass constant, then an exponential factor is introduced to reduce high-volume overestimation.

governing_equations.source_expression: Leaf mass = volume of geometric solid * leaf mass constant
governing_equations.purpose: Convert modeled crown volume to leaf mass.

governing_equations.source_expression: LM = V*LMC = (1/3) pi r^2 h * 280 for cone oak example
governing_equations.purpose: Instantiate the basic model for a conical oak crown.
Reduce predicted mass as crown volume increases.

steps: Measure crown height and mean radius.
Calculate V under each candidate solid.
Multiply V by LMC.

algorithm.convergence_criteria: Closed-form calculation; no iterative convergence applies.

assumptions: An ideal solid captures crown volume.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: Measured masses permit comparison, but units printed for LMC are implausible, lambda lacks dimensional calibration, and model choice uses mean ratios that can hide individual error.

models.computational_cost: Constant per solid per tree; six closed-form candidates are evaluated for each tree.
strengths: Compares several geometric assumptions on a common dataset.
limitations: Mean prediction ratio near one is treated as accuracy without dispersion.
The attenuation coefficient is chosen without fitting or units.
Crown shape and within-crown density variation are oversimplified.

dependency_edges.handoff: The four descriptors and cluster-derived labels become BPNN predictors and supervised targets.
Local illumination I from the two-dimensional canopy field becomes the independent variable in the leaf-size response.
The 14-tree measured leaf-mass dataset assembled for volumetric comparison is reused to fit and compare the DBH quadratic.
